newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade students fight battle of wills with police.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade students fight battle of wills with police.

text.p: Student protesters in Belgrade fought a battle of wills with Serbian police on Thursday, vowing to blockade their cordons until they let them march.
Demonstrators forced police to back off at one location, then re-formed in front of a second cordon in a street near Belgrade's ancient fortress.
The group of about 200 students performed a folk dance, and Belgraders gathered on the other side of the cordon to support them. The students asked them not to provoke the police.
Diplomats fear provocateurs could spark an incident to give a pretext for a police crackdown and ban on rallies.
The government banned protest marches after clashes between pro-government and opposition demonstrators on December 24.
The students have organised groups of demonstrators to rotate every hour and vow they will continue until an official statement was issued saying police would not block the streets.
They appealed to the people of Belgrade to come out and support them throughout the night.
Thursday marked the 53rd day of protests against the cancellation of local election results by President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists last November.

The protests have shaken the foundations of leftist rule in Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia which has been led by Communists and their successors, Milosevic's Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), since 1945.
On Wednesday, Milosevic conceded that the opposition Zajedno coalition had won in Nis, Serbia's second city, but Zajedno leaders vowed protests would continue until all their claims were met.

"The people of Nis said that if the November 17 election results are not recognised by January 14 ,they will get into 2,000 or 3,000 cars and travel to Belgrade," one Zajedno leader, Zoran Djindjic, told a rally of about 20,000 people in Republic Square.
The opposition says it won 41 seats in Nis, not the 37 awarded by the government on Wednesday.

"The fact that the Socialists gave us 37 mandates in Nis indicates that they plan to mount various manipulations later, in Nis as well as other towns, all in order to strip us gradually of our election victory," Djindjic said.
Milosevic's government promised on Wednesday to rectify "every irregularity" in connection with its annulment of opposition election victories in 15 Serbian cities including Nis and Belgrade.
"Behind us: Serbia, before us: the police, and a little further on: Europe. Police -- let Serbia become part of Europe!" read one banner at Thursday's rally.

France added to the international chorus of disapproval of Milosevic, saying it would send an envoy to Belgrade to urge his government to heed the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's confirmation of the opposition wins.

"The Serbian government must admit, unconditionally and without qualification, that the opposition was victorious in 15 Serbian cities including the capital, and in eight of Belgrade's districts," said foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt.

He said Paul Poulade, director of continental Europe at the Foreign Ministry, would meet Serbian Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic and opposition leaders during a three-day visit beginning on Saturday.
The government responded to the OSCE report by admitting Zajedno had won in nine wards of Belgrade and three smaller provincial cities.
But it said nothing about Belgrade's policy-making municipal assembly and contended that in the other cities no party won a majority or the results were inconclusive and required further examination.
